items.title: <div data-chronoton-summary="<ul><br><li><strong>Demand is driving the boom:</strong> Micr
items.summary:
Earlier this month, Microsoft launched Copilot Health, a new space within its Copilot app where users will be able to connect their medical records and ask specific questions about their health. A couple of days earlier, Amazon had announced that Health AI, an LLM-based tool previously restricted to members of its One Medical service, would now be widely available. These products join the ranks of ChatGPT Health, which OpenAI released back in January, and Anthropic’s Claude, which can access user health records if granted permission. Health AI for the masses is officially a trend. 

There’s a clear demand for chatbots that provide health advice, given how hard it is for many people to access it through existing medical systems. And some research suggests that current LLMs are capable of making safe and useful recommendations. But researchers say that these tools should be more rigorously evaluated by independent experts, ideally before they are widely released. 

In a high-stakes area like health, trusting companies to evaluate their own products could prove unwise, especially if those evaluations aren’t made available for external expert review. And even if the companies are doing quality, rigorous research—which some, including OpenAI, do seem to be—they might still have blind spots that the broader research community could help to fill.

“To the extent that you always are going to need more health care, I think we should definitely be chasing every route that works,” says Andrew Bean, a doctoral candidate at the Oxford Internet Institute. “It’s entirely plausible to me that these models have reached a point where they’re actually worth rolling out.”

“But,” he adds, “the evidence base really needs to be there.”

Tipping points 

To hear developers tell it, these health products are now being released because large language models have indeed reached a point where they can effectively provide medical advice. Dominic King, the vice president of health at Microsoft AI and a former surgeon, cites AI advancement as a core reason why the company’s health team was formed, and why Copilot Health now exists. “We’ve seen this enormous progress in the capabilities of generative AI to be able to answer health questions and give good responses,” he says.

But that’s only half the story, according to King. The other key factor is demand. Shortly before Copilot Health was launched, Microsoft published a report, and an accompanying blog post, detailing how people used Copilot for health advice. The company says it receives 50 million health questions each day, and health is the most popular discussion topic on the Copilot mobile app.

Other AI companies have noticed, and responded to, this trend. “Even before our health products, we were seeing just a rapid, rapid increase in the rate of people using ChatGPT for health-related questions,” says Karan Singhal, who leads OpenAI’s Health AI team. (OpenAI and Microsoft have a long-standing partnership, and Copilot is powered by OpenAI’s models.)

It’s possible that people simply prefer posing their health problems to a nonjudgmental bot that’s available to them 24-7. But many experts interpret this pattern in light of the current state of the health-care system. “There is a reason that these tools exist and they have a position in the overall landscape,” says Girish Nadkarni, chief AI officer​ at the Mount Sinai Health System. “That’s because access to health care is hard, and it’s particularly hard for certain populations.”

The virtuous vision of consumer-facing LLM health chatbots hinges on the possibility that they could improve user health while reducing pressure on the health-care system. That might involve helping users decide whether or not they need medical attention, a task known as triage. If chatbot triage works, then patients who need emergency care might seek it out earlier than they would have otherwise, and patients with more mild concerns might feel comfortable managing their symptoms at home with the chatbot’s advice rather than unnecessarily busying emergency rooms and doctor’s offices.

But a recent, widely discussed study from Nadkarni and other researchers at Mount Sinai found that ChatGPT Health sometimes recommends too much care for mild conditions and fails to identify emergencies. Though Singhal and  some other experts have suggested that its methodology might not provide a complete picture of ChatGPT Health’s capabilities, the study has surfaced concerns about how little external evaluation these tools see before being released to the public.

Most of the academic experts interviewed for this piece agreed that LLM health chatbots could have real upsides, given how little access to health care some people have. But all six of them expressed concerns that these tools are being launched without testing from independent researchers to assess whether they are safe. While some advertised uses of these tools, such as recommending exercise plans or suggesting questions that a user might ask a doctor, are relatively harmless, others carry clear risks. Triage is one; another is asking a chatbot to provide a diagnosis or a treatment plan. 

The ChatGPT Health interface includes a prominent disclaimer stating that it is not intended for diagnosis or treatment, and the announcements for Copilot Health and Amazon’s Health AI include similar warnings. But those warnings are easy to ignore. “We all know that people are going to use it for diagnosis and management,” says Adam Rodman, an internal medicine physician and researcher at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and a visiting researcher at Google.

Medical testing

Companies say they are testing the chatbots to ensure that they provide safe responses the vast majority of the time. OpenAI has designed and released HealthBench, a benchmark that scores LLMs on how they respond in realistic health-related conversations—though the conversations themselves are LLM-generated. When GPT-5, which powers both ChatGPT Health and Copilot Health, was released last year, OpenAI reported the model’s HealthBench scores: It did substantially better than previous OpenAI models, though its overall performance was far from perfect. 

But evaluations like HealthBench have limitations. In a study published last month, Bean—the Oxford doctoral candidate—and his colleagues found that even if an LLM can accurately identify a medical condition from a fictional written scenario on its own, a non-expert user who is given the scenario and asked to determine the condition with LLM assistance might figure it out only a third of the time. If they lack medical expertise, users might not know which parts of a scenario—or their real-life experience—are important to include in their prompt, or they might misinterpret the information that an LLM gives them.

Bean says that this performance gap could be significant for OpenAI’s models. In the original HealthBench study, the company reported that its models performed relatively poorly in conversations that required them to seek more information from the user. If that’s the case, then users who don’t have enough medical knowledge to provide a health chatbot with the information that it needs from the get-go might get unhelpful or inaccurate advice.

Singhal, the OpenAI health lead, notes that the company’s current GPT-5 series of models, which had not yet been released when the original HealthBench study was conducted, do a much better job of soliciting additional information than their predecessors. However, OpenAI has reported that GPT-5.4, the current flagship, is actually worse at seeking context than GPT-5.2, an earlier version.

Ideally, Bean says, health chatbots would be subjected to controlled tests with human users, as they were in his study, before being released to the public. That might be a heavy lift, particularly given how fast the AI world moves and how long human studies can take. Bean’s own study used GPT-4o, which came out almost a year ago and is now outdated. 

Earlier this month, Google released a study that meets Bean’s standards. In the study, patients discussed medical concerns with the company’s Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), a medical LLM chatbot that is not yet available to the public, before meeting with a human physician. Overall, AMIE’s diagnoses were just as accurate as physicians’, and none of the conversations raised major safety concerns for researchers. 

Despite the encouraging results, Google isn’t planning to release AMIE anytime soon. “While the research has advanced, there are significant limitations that must be addressed before real-world translation of systems for diagnosis and treatment, including further research into equity, fairness, and safety testing,” wrote Alan Karthikesalingam, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, in an email. Google did recently reveal that Health100, a health platform it is building in partnership with CVS, will include an AI assistant powered by its flagship Gemini models, though that tool will presumably not be intended for diagnosis or treatment.

Rodman, who led the AMIE study with Karthikesalingam, doesn’t think such extensive, multiyear studies are necessarily the right approach for chatbots like ChatGPT Health and Copilot Health. “There’s lots of reasons that the clinical trial paradigm doesn’t always work in generative AI,” he says. “And that’s where this benchmarking conversation comes in. Are there benchmarks [from] a trusted third party that we can agree are meaningful, that the labs can hold themselves to?”

They key there is “third party.” No matter how extensively companies evaluate their own products, it’s tough to trust their conclusions completely. Not only does a third-party evaluation bring impartiality, but if there are many third parties involved, it also helps protect against blind spots.

OpenAI’s Singhal says he’s strongly in favor of external evaluation. “We try our best to support the community,” he says. “Part of why we put out HealthBench was actually to give the community and other model developers an example of what a very good evaluation looks like.” 

Given how expensive it is to produce a high-quality evaluation, he says, he’s skeptical that any individual academic laboratory would be able to produce what he calls “the one evaluation to rule them all.” But he does speak highly of efforts that academic groups have made to bring preexisting and novel evaluations together into comprehensive evaluations suites—such as Stanford’s MedHELM framework, which tests models on a wide variety of medical tasks. Currently, OpenAI’s GPT-5 holds the highest MedHELM score.

Nigam Shah, a professor of medicine at Stanford University who led the MedHELM project, says it has limitations. In particular, it only evaluates individual chatbot responses, but someone who’s seeking medical advice from a chatbot tool might engage it in a multi-turn, back-and-forth conversation. He says that he and some collaborators are gearing up to build an evaluation that can score those complex conversations, but that it will take time, and money. “You and I have zero ability to stop these companies from releasing [health-oriented products], so they’re going to do whatever they damn please,” he says. “The only thing people like us can do is find a way to fund the benchmark.”

No one interviewed for this article argued that health LLMs need to perform perfectly on third-party evaluations in order to be released. Doctors themselves make mistakes—and for someone who has only occasional access to a doctor, a consistently accessible LLM that sometimes messes up could still be a huge improvement over the status quo, as long as its errors aren’t too grave. 

With the current state of the evidence, however, it’s impossible to know for sure whether the currently available tools do in fact constitute an improvement, or whether their risks outweigh their benefits.

items.title: 🚀 5 AI Building Blocks Every Software Engineer Should Know in 2026
items.summary:
🚀 5 AI Building Blocks Every Software Engineer Should Know in 2026

Want to build real AI applications instead of just using ChatGPT?

You need to understand these 5 concepts. 🧵👇

1️⃣ Large Language Models (LLMs) 🧠

The brain behind modern AI applications.

Models like GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama can:
• Understand natural language
• Generate code and content
• Reason through complex problems
• Power intelligent applications

2️⃣ Embedding Models 🔍
Turn text and other data into numerical vectors.
They power:
• Semantic search
• Similarity matching
• Recommendation systems
• Knowledge retrieval

3️⃣ RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) 📚

Connect LLMs to your own business data.

Instead of relying only on training data, AI retrieves relevant information from your documents or databases.

Essential for enterprise AI and SaaS applications.
4️⃣ AI Agent Harnesses 🤖
Move beyond chatbots.
Agent harnesses provide the tools, memory, orchestration, and execution environment that allow AI agents to perform tasks.
Think Claude Code, coding agents, and automated business workflows.

5️⃣ World Models 🌍

AI systems that learn how physical environments behave.

Important for:
• Robotics
• Autonomous vehicles
• Physical AI
• Simulation and planning

💡 The Big Takeaway

The future of AI engineering isn't just about choosing the best LLM.

It's about combining models, retrieval, tools, and intelligent workflows to solve real-world problems.

I'm a software engineer building AI SaaS applications in Sydney, Australia. 🇦🇺

Which of these 5 technologies are you currently learning or building with?

#AI #AIEngineering #SoftwareEngineering #BuildInPublic

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Apology May Be the Only Correct Use of AI - The Atlantic
items.summary:
People (me) are always saying about AI, “This is a solution looking for a problem!” and “Who would possibly want to delegate things like knowing information about your childrenor creating works of art to a third-party series of zeroes and ones?” But there are some things in life that nobody wants to do, such as get a root canal, amputate a limb, or deal with your cable provider. Or, perhaps, apologize simultaneously to your employees and your wife of 40 years for jeopardizing your business and [...] Look, I just want to say that if NVIDIA CEO and reported spy-plot target Jensen Huang did get help from AI to write an apology email to his family and company about his affair (he’s said he uses AI to help write all of his first drafts), this might be the one use of AI that makes sense to me. [...] Now I am worried, based on Jensen Huang’s claim that this was “completely normal and not unusual” and an NVIDIA spokesperson’s insistence that his interactions with the alleged spy were “not unusual” that, actually, we’ll be seeing multiple emails like this. Finally, organic demand for AI! If so, the template will get better and better—that is, if we can still use the chips.

items.title: Việt Nam - Nhật Bản hoàn tất chuyển giao công nghệ tế bào trị ung thư
items.summary:
Công nghệ tế bào gốc trung mô (MSC) hiện được nghiên cứu, phát triển trong nhiều hướng ứng dụng liên quan đến bệnh lý tim mạch, thần kinh (đột quỵ, sa sút trí tuệ), tiểu đường, bệnh phổi tắc nghẽn mạn tính (COPD), trẻ hóa da… Giải pháp tế bào miễn dịch tự nhiên (NK) mở ra cơ hội ứng dụng mới trong miễn dịch trị liệu, có thể được phối hợp với các phương pháp điều trị ung thư đa mô thức khác, như phẫu thuật, hóa trị, xạ trị và điều trị đích. [...] Hai bên lựa chọn chuyển giao các công nghệ tế bào thế hệ mới, được Tập đoàn Y tế Grandsoul, Nhật Bản nghiên cứu, phát triển và ứng dụng. Bộ Y tế, Lao động và Phúc lợi Nhật Bản (MHLW) đã phê duyệt, cấp phép ứng dụng chính thức nhiều năm tại nước này. Trọng tm gồm hai nhóm: công nghệ phn lập, nuôi cấy, biệt hóa chọn lọc tế bào gốc trung mô có nguồn gốc từ mô mỡ (Mesenchymal Stem Cells - MSC) và công nghệ phn lập nuôi cấy, biệt hóa chọn lọc tế bào miễn dịch tự nhiên NK (Natural Killer cells) điều [...] ### Từ tiếp nhận công nghệ đến năng lực tự chủ tại Việt Nam

Ông Ngô Chí Dũng, Chủ tịch HĐQT Hệ thống Bệnh viện Đa khoa Tm Anh, cho biết việc hoàn tất chuyển giao công nghệ tế bào gốc và tế bào miễn dịch từ Nhật Bản là dấu mốc quan trọng không chỉ trong hợp tác y tế hai nước, mà còn là kết nối công nghệ, thiết lập mạng lưới chuyên gia vì mục tiêu chung là chăm sóc sức khỏe cho người dn.

items.title: Cây trồng công nghệ sinh học - Cơ hội tăng trưởng mới nông nghiệp theo hướng xanh
items.summary:
Ứng dụng công nghệ sinh học, công nghệ gen trong nông nghiệp mở ra những cơ hội mới cho ngành trồng trọt. Ảnh minh họa: Báo Lm Đồng

Hoàn thiện hành lang pháp lý, thúc đẩy công nghệ sinh học trong nông nghiệp

Theo TS Nguyễn Văn Long, Vụ trưởng Vụ Khoa học và Công nghệ (Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường), trong bối cảnh nông nghiệp phải đối mặt với biến đổi khí hậu, dịch bệnh và yêu cầu phát triển bền vững, việc nghiên cứu, làm chủ và ứng dụng các công nghệ tiên tiến càng trở nên cấp thiết. [...] Tổng diện tích canh tác lũy kế trong gần ba thập kỷ đạt khoảng 3,75 tỷ ha trên toàn cầu, cho thấy quy mô ứng dụng ngày càng mở rộng và sự chấp nhận ngày càng rộng rãi đối với công nghệ này trên thế giới. Đáng chú ý, việc ứng dụng cy trồng biến đổi gen không còn chỉ tập trung tại các quốc gia phát triển. Các nước đang phát triển, đặc biệt tại Mỹ Latinh, chu Á và chu Phi ngày càng đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc mở rộng ứng dụng công nghệ này. [...] Đy là những kết quả bước đầu cho thấy khả năng tiếp nhận và ứng dụng công nghệ sinh học trong sản xuất nông nghiệp. Tuy nhiên, trước yêu cầu đổi mới mô hình tăng trưởng, vấn đề đặt ra không chỉ là mở rộng diện tích ứng dụng mà còn phải nng cao năng lực nghiên cứu, chủ động công nghệ và phát triển các sản phẩm có giá trị gia tăng cao.

items.title: Định hướng thúc đẩy ngoại giao khoa học và công nghệ
items.summary:
Để phát huy hơn nữa tiềm năng này, bà Đỗ Quỳnh Hoa cho biết, Bộ Khoa học và Công nghệ cần triển khai đồng bộ một số định hướng trọng tm. items.title: Ohio State and Microsoft announced a five-year partnership, expanding AI use in health care
items.summary:
Azure could allow researchers to access “appropriate, de-identified data” while protecting privacy, according to the press release. 

The partnership will use AI, including Dragon Copilot, to reduce administrative work, such as drafting clinical notes from conversations between providers and patients, Kennedy said. 

“However, AI is not the care provider,” Kennedy said. “AI is simply a tool in the toolkit to allow you to get the focus where you want it on your patient.” [...] Both organizations are also exploring artificial intelligence-supported tumor-board workflows that could bring together pathology, imaging, genomic information and patients’ medical histories, allowing clinicians to collaborate on cases and plan treatments, the press release stated. [...] Areas of focus include developing “smart hospital” technology, moving clinical workloads to the cloud, creating a unified data system and using artificial intelligence to support health care providers, John J. Warner, CEO of the Wexner Medical Center and executive vice president, said. 

“This is an opportunity to help reimagine the future of health care, not simply respond to it,” Warner said.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Apology May Be the Only Correct Use of AI - The Atlantic
items.summary:
People (me) are always saying about AI, “This is a solution looking for a problem!” and “Who would possibly want to delegate things like knowing information about your childrenor creating works of art to a third-party series of zeroes and ones?” But there are some things in life that nobody wants to do, such as get a root canal, amputate a limb, or deal with your cable provider. Or, perhaps, apologize simultaneously to your employees and your wife of 40 years for jeopardizing your business and [...] Now I am worried, based on Jensen Huang’s claim that this was “completely normal and not unusual” and an NVIDIA spokesperson’s insistence that his interactions with the alleged spy were “not unusual” that, actually, we’ll be seeing multiple emails like this. Finally, organic demand for AI! If so, the template will get better and better—that is, if we can still use the chips.

items.title: How Robots are Delivering ROI in Mexico?
items.summary:
Articulated robots: Multi-axis robotic arms used for welding, painting, assembly, and heavy material handling. They remain particularly relevant to automotive production.
 SCARA robots: Systems designed for high-speed, precise horizontal movements, frequently used in electronics assembly, component insertion, and packaging.
 Delta robots: Parallel-arm systems suited to rapid picking, sorting, and packaging, particularly in food and consumer goods manufacturing. [...] However, the evolution of industrial robotics is changing the investment equation. Historically, manufacturers deployed robots primarily for repetitive, high-volume operations, including welding vehicle bodies, painting components, and transferring materials between production stations. Modern systems increasingly combine robotic manipulators with machine vision, sensors, AI, and software that allows manufacturers to change production parameters without rebuilding entire automation systems. [...] The most commercially established applications in Mexico are articulated industrial arms, particularly those deployed in welding, painting, assembly, and material handling. These systems can operate continuously, execute repetitive movements with consistent precision, and integrate into production lines. Their adoption is especially relevant to automotive manufacturers, where production volumes and quality requirements can justify substantial capital expenditure.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5: Accelerating Physical Intelligence — Google DeepMind
items.summary:
Dexterity: Our robots can perform significantly more tasks with greater performance and dexterity — from using everyday tools to handling delicate, flexible objects.
 Reliability: During a real-world proof-of-concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines, our models helped Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid pick and pack automotive parts with a 96% success rate. This could enable robots to take on monotonous work, to enable technicians to focus on complex build tasks. [...] Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think, reason over multiple steps, and take action adapting to changes. In this proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 autonomously performs automotive kitting: the repetitive, physically taxing task of sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the exact order needed for each vehicle on the line. Offloading this monotonous prep work helps keep the assembly line moving, [...] With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks — such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.

items.title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak" - Ars Technica
items.summary: DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate. [...] Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. [...] Overall, Gemini Robotics 2.5 manages a 30 to 100 percent higher success rate compared to the last version. It’s also 20 to 30 percent faster. But that’s based on laboratory testing. Google partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to see how capable this AI is when faced with the uncertainty of the world outside robotics labs. The Gemini-powered Apollo 2 robots kitted automotive parts in a few European factories, reaching a 96 percent success rate.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Exclusive: OpenAI targets Microsoft's GitHub with deal
items.summary:
OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer, a developer tools startup whose technology is already embedded in Codex, the company told Axios exclusively.

Why it matters:OpenAI is joining a slew of companies challenging Microsoft's GitHub as AI agents take on more coding work. The platform has acted as a central repository and nerve center for software development for many years.

Zoom out:GitHub has faced a number of reliability issues and outages as AI coding has taken off. [...] Financial terms were not disclosed. Pierre's open-source projects will remain open-source.

Between the lines:Earlier this week, OpenAI revealed Pando, built to handle the explosion of code generated by AI agents.

   OpenAI says Pando reduced the time needed to push code changes by nearly 80%. 
   The company is now exploring ways to make the technology available to customers. [...] Cursor, now owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, launched GitHub rival Origin in August.
   Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, who launched a new coding startup, announced a competing product last month.
   Microsoft owns nearly a quarter of OpenAI, although the two companies also compete in a variety of ways, a dynamic that is common across the competitive AI landscape.

Driving the news: OpenAI plans to integrate Pierre's Code Storage function into Codex, where Pierre's technology is already used.

items.title: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers | Reuters
items.summary:
OpenAI officials, along with many of their peers in tech, ​have spent the last ⁠two years trying to build ties with the administration of US President Donald Trump in hopes of shaping federal policy around AI.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman donated $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee and later attended Trump's second inauguration. Last year, Brockman donated $25 million in his personal capacity to ⁠a Trump ​super PAC. [...] SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Stunning ​victories by Democrats in US midterm elections this week have been interpreted by many as Americans repudiating tech ‌industry plans to build data centers across the country. OpenAI has now embarked on new strategies to change their minds.

The AI lab on Thursday laid out policies — in the works since August — intended to help the company build more trust with local communities and convince them that data centers will ​benefit them. [...] One OpenAI facility in southern Ohio is expected ​to create 2,500 long-term jobs with an average annual salary of $80,000, he said.

Partners such as Oracle (ORCL.N) are building and own much ​of OpenAI's data center infrastructure, with the capacity dedicated to the startup.
